article_text:
自画像 47KMの窓

劇場公開日： 2026年11月15日

解説・あらすじ

中国湖北省の山あいにある村「47KM村」に10年以上通い続ける監督ジャン・モンチーが、村の老人たちの記憶と子どもたちの成長を記録したドキュメンタリー「自画像 47KM」シリーズの第8作。 毛沢東の肖像が掲げられた部屋で、ひとりの老人が革命に明け暮れた自らの半生を語り始める。一方、15歳になった少女は村の老人たちの家々を訪ね、薄暗い部屋で彼らの肖像を描いていく。やがて彼女は、崩れかけた村の壁にも老人の顔を描き始める。少女の絵は閉ざされた家に開かれた窓となり、老人たちの記憶と荒れ果てた部屋に一筋の光を差し込んでいく。そして厳しい冬が明けるころ、村は色彩に染まっていく。 2010年から毎年村に通って撮影し、北京で編集するという制作を続けてきたジャン・モンチーは、2020年には村に家を建てて移り住んだ。本作は山形国際ドキュメンタリー映画祭2019のインターナショナル・コンペティション部門で上映。日本初上映の5本を含むシリーズ全10本をそろえた特集上映の1本として、2026年11月7～20日にポレポレ東中野で公開される。

2019年製作／111分／中国 原題または英題：Self-portrait: Sphinx in 47 KM 劇場公開日：2026年11月15日

監督

article_text:
Sotheby’s kicked off the November marquee sales with a doubleheader on Monday evening that generated $378.7 million across 74 lots. The top-line results look solid, but a sluggish second half seemed to further illustrate the choosy mood among collectors right now.

The nearly three-hour marathon started strong with the dedicated sale from the collection of cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum. It was a white-glove result, with all 24 works sold for a hammer total of $90.9 million. With fees, the sale landed at $110 million, just a shade above the presale high estimate of $109 million.

The Baum sale was a lively affair from the start. After the first lot— Roy Lichtenstein ’s 1983 cut-paper work Two Paintings: Sleeping Muse (Study) —sparked a four-minute contest among three specialists and a bidder in the room, CEO Charles Stewart strode over to Gareth Jones, the house’s chief marketing officer, and said of the $3.8 million total, “Well, that’s a good start.” Three lots later, a Lucio Fontana copper canvas with a glorious cut down the middle ignited another bidding war, the bids ricocheting among three bidders in the room. It hammered at $3.5 million, or $4.4 million with fees, well above the $3 million high estimate.

Oliver Barker, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, handled the proceedings with panache, making even a fairly ordinary stretch of bidding feel brisk. Amid the bidding for Lot 7, Andy Warhol’s 1984 painting The Scream (After Munch) , he teased Jacqueline Wachter, chairwoman of private sales, for taking a bit too long with her phone bidder, asking whether she was “doing her shopping or doing her conversions.” Then he quipped to the audience, “Amazon is always open. As is Sotheby’s Dot Com.” It was a little sharp, perhaps, but it got a laugh and helped lighten the mood as the sale began to drag.

The crowded salesroom was a who’s who of the art trade: Dominique Lévy, Brett Gorvy, Amalia Dayan, David Schrader, Emmanuel Di Donna, Christophe Van de Weghe, and Gagosian Art Advisory’s Bernard Lagrange were just a few of the heavies in attendance.

In the end, six works hammered above their estimates and another 10 landed in range, with spirited bidding throughout, both in the room and on the phone. Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest led the sale at $19.3 million, followed by Mark Rothko’s Untitled at $17.7 million and Ed Ruscha’s Dimple at $11.6 million. The Baums had bought the Mitchell privately in 1986 for just $65,000, making its sale price nearly 300 times what they paid. The Rothko, which they acquired for $115,000 in 1983, brought more than 150 times its purchase price. Not bad for a few decades of collecting. The final lot in the sale, Mario Merz’s neon sculpture Iguana , sold well below its estimate, but that did little to dampen the enthusiasm, as the room erupted in applause.

The Now and Contemporary sale that followed was considerably less celebratory. Of the 53 lots originally offered, three were withdrawn before the sale, and another five went unsold: works by Kerry James Marshall, Ellsworth Kelly, Roy Lichtenstein, and Keith Haring, and, curiously, a Formula One race car . Tom Eddison, head of contemporary art at Sotheby’s London, who took over auctioneering duties for the sale, said the car was a first for the auction house, and it required a lengthy preamble explaining that the sale was subject to the terms of service of RM Sotheby’s, the house’s classic-car affiliate. The car garnered a handful of bids but failed to reach its low estimate before Eddison declared it unsold. It may be some time before Sotheby’s tries that experiment again.

That’s not to say the results for the contemporary sale were lackluster. When all was said and done, the sale garnered a hammer total of $224.8 million. With fees, the total climbed to $268.8 million, within the presale aggregate estimate of $226.2 million to $323 million, and well above the equivalent sale in November 2025, which generated $178.5 million. Of course, we should note that last year’s sale followed the trove of works from the late cosmetics heir Leonard Lauder, which generated an eye-watering $527.5 million. Alas, not every season sees three Klimts hit the block.

Of the 45 lots that sold, a full 14 hammered above their presale estimates, and another 24 landed in range. Still, while there always seemed to be a handful of bidders for each sold lot, with Eddison darting his hands left, right, and center, most works hammered after only a minute or two.

The most protracted bidding wars came somewhat early. A six-minute contest among four specialists for Jeff Koons’s 1991 sculpture Bob-Tail ended with contemporary art specialist Bame Fierro March winning the lot for a hammer price of $9 million. At $10.7 million with fees, that’s good for just over three times the high estimate. (Is Koons’s market trending back up, or do collectors just really like an adorable English sheepdog?) Seven lots later, Agnes Martin’s cream canvas Desert , from the collection of Lenore and Bernard Greenberg, sold after a six-minute duel between contemporary art specialist Alya Sama and Lisa Dennison, chairman of the Americas. Dennison won on a $9.2 million hammer bid, or $11.3 million with fees, comfortably above the $8 million high estimate. And Andy Warhol’s 1964–65 painting Flowers fetched $18.2 million with fees against a $10 million to $15 million estimate.

Mark the Warhol and Koons results as green shoots for a market that’s spent much of the past two years playing it safe. Neither artist has had the easiest time in the secondary market lately, which makes those results particularly interesting. Something to watch going forward, especially for Koons.

After the sale, Dennison pointed to the continued strength of early Martin paintings, which have been outperforming expectations for several seasons.

Art adviser Ed Dolman similarly found the night’s results encouraging. In a text message toward the end of the sale, he said, “The best works always do fine, [but] buyers were taking some risks again.”

Dolman also pointed to the depth of bidding. While 29 of the 45 sold lots in the contemporary sale had guarantees—as did every work in the Baum sale—those guarantors were often outbid on Monday night. Buyers, it seemed, were willing to go a little further.

Not that everything was suddenly flying off the walls. Lichtenstein’s Reflections on ‘Painter and Model,’ the top lot of the contemporary sale at $24.7 million with fees, came in well short of the high end of its $20 million to $30 million estimate. Willem de Kooning’s Water…Soft Banks of a Window (Untitled VIII) brought $20.3 million, just above its $20 million low estimate, while Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I made $17.1 million against a $15 million to $20 million estimate.

The buzziest result of the night was no doubt for Yayoi Kusama ’s 1960 painting No. 3P.B. , which hammered for $12.5 million after 10 bids spread across four minutes. With fees, the result came to $15.1 million, just above the $15 million high estimate, and good for a new record for the artist, who died in August. About 10 lots later, another of her “Infinity Nets” paintings, Infinity Nets (OZEH) , sold for a hammer price of $2.5 million, or $3.1 million with fees, just a shade above the $3 million high estimate. That work, a white canvas measuring roughly 6½ by 8½ feet, is far more recent, dating to 2011. And if you missed out on those two Kusamas, have no fear: Another 10 works of hers will hit the block over the rest of marquee week. Five are from her long-running “Infinity Nets” series.

Yet, for all the strong prices, the second half of the contemporary sale was a slog. With Eddison at the rostrum, the pace slowed considerably. Bids were drawn out, pauses stretched on, and even works that eventually fetched impressive prices seemed to take an age to get there. A few market watchers wondered whether such a sluggish tempo might discourage bidders, particularly on works that didn’t have much competition to begin with. It was an odd contrast: a sale that sometimes felt as though it was struggling to find its rhythm, even as buyers were spending millions more than expected.

To Nina Del Rio, an art adviser and auction house veteran, the results looked remarkably strong, particularly given the subdued energy in the second half of the sale. Still, she said, there hasn’t been much evidence of a shift in the market. At least not a fundamental one. Buyers appear to be behaving much as they did in May, when the best works attracted serious money but enthusiasm for younger artists remained muted. A few years ago, the Now sale was where collectors went to get their hands on artists whose waiting lists seemed impossible to crack. That sense of urgency has largely disappeared.

What collectors do seem willing to pay for is scarcity. Del Rio pointed to the modern masterpieces coming up later in the week, the sort of works that rarely appear at auction and may not come around again for decades. Among them is Wednesday’s sale of the Blaquier Collection , a group of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterpieces said to be worth around $450 million, and a $180 million Van Gogh suddenly subject to a last-minute restitution claim.

Dennison warned against reading too much into a single evening. Given the current mood, starting the week with contemporary art rather than a mix of modern and contemporary masterpieces makes it harder to judge the market as a whole. And while works in the $10 million to $20 million range performed well, the sale lacked the $30 million, $40 million, and $50 million trophies that drive enthusiasm across the whole week.

As for that Formula One car, Dennison said the result left her scratching her head. The last bid offered, $3.9 million, was just under the $4 million low estimate. Did the interested buyer really think the $100,000 gap was too wide to bridge?

There is a risk to putting something unexpected into a contemporary art sale. But, as Dennison pointed out, sometimes it works, as when Christie’s sold the Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton “Stan” during its 20th Century Evening Sale in 2020 for $31.8 million, nearly quadruple the high estimate.

Sotheby’s shouldn’t give up on the idea. There’s something appealing about an evening sale that doesn’t draw a firm boundary around paintings and sculptures. Not every experiment works the first time, or even the second. And if the object is truly one-of-a-kind, buyers are ready to shell out the cash.
excerpt_original: The Ted and Ruth Baum collection sold every lot, and Yayoi Kusama set a new auction record, but a slow second half showed collectors are still choosy.

article_text:
日本のみならず、世界からの注目も集まる「禅」をテーマとした展覧会が各地で開催されています。京都有数の禅宗寺院の至宝が一堂に介する注目展から、アニメ作品を通して気軽に禅の世界に親しめる展覧会まで、多彩なラインナップです。禅に対して難解なイメージを抱く方も多いかと思いますが、心惹かれる作品や親近感がわく書画などを通して、その世界に気軽に触れてみてはいかがでしょう。日常や仕事にも活きる禅の言葉、教えを持ち帰ることができるかもしれません。

開創700年記念 特別展「大徳寺 本朝無双之禅苑」 東京国立博物館で12月6日まで 洛北の巨刹の歴史を物語る至宝の数々が一堂に

「白隠ワールド―細川護立コレクションのはじまり―」東京・永青文庫で11月29日まで 白隠の世界にどっぷりはまる

『禅とジブリ』京都展 京都市京セラ美術館 新館 東山キューブで12月6日まで ジブリ作品の世界に没入しながら禅の言葉と視点を自由に持ち帰る

「良寛さん―その人と禅―」京都・細見美術館で11月8日まで 慈愛と禅の精神が詰まった珠玉の作品群にふれる

秋の企画展 大本山 佛通寺展 ふくやま草戸千軒ミュージアム（広島県立歴史博物館）で11月29日まで まもなく創建630周年を迎える佛通寺の貴重な文化財を紹介

◇あわせて読みたい

【座談会】「この世は美しかった」と旅立つために――医科大学がリベラルアーツセンターを開く理由とは 京都の禅宗寺院の妙心寺退蔵院で歴史学者、禅僧、医師がトーク【PR】

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班）
article_author: アート・エキシビション・ジャパン

article_text:
“A yōkai is a fallen god,” wrote Yanagita Kunio, the father of Japanese folklore studies. The line already accompanied Yuji Watanabe’s exhibition “Yōkai” at 229 Gallery in Tokyo in September 2024, and it opens every door. A god knocked off his pedestal, then, driven out of the shrines, taking refuge behind folding screens, in faded kimonos, under old futons. A harsh fall from grace. Sacred monsters, in the literal sense.

Yuji Watanabe knows the power of metamorphosis. Trained in Japan, he studied photography in New York, returned to Tokyo, then settled in Paris in 2012. He shoots fashion stories for international magazines, a world where a coat is enough to change a silhouette (creatures demand more). Alongside it grew a personal practice, analog and stubborn. As he explains, the fantastic needs the real in order to exist: without that share of reality at the moment of creation, he himself stops feeling the fantastic, hence his attachment to analog processes. The large-format camera, the light, the chemistry, all of it.

What he photographs: ghosts in flesh and blood. A head drifting away at the end of an endless neck, over a folding screen painted with mountains ( Rokurokubi ). A face as smooth as an egg, arms raised in a striped kimono ( Noppera-bō ). A woman swallowed by her own hair ( Kejōrō ). Two heads for a single body ( Dōmokōmo ). A tattered futon that takes on a life of its own ( Boroboroton ). And Miku (未来, “future”), a creature invented by Yuji Watanabe, whose features slide across the face like dripping wax. Miku, according to curator Charli Sas, “carries the tradition into the present.” The dread lies in a slight shift, like a frame hung crooked in a hotel room.

A risky bet, folklore staged by a fashion photographer? It depends: look at Irving Penn. Still, the danger has a name, costume, and Mendon , with its spiral headdress set on a straw skirt, comes close. Yuji Watanabe wards it off through material. The 8×10 Polaroid gives the bodies a velvety grain, deep blacks, frayed edges, the patina of an old print found at the bottom of a trunk. The film itself joins the world of ghosts.

Is there anybody there? The séance question is put, this time, to the landscapes. For this new series, Yuji Watanabe traveled across Japan with One Instant peel-apart film, a process in which the positive is separated from the negative by hand, leaving burns, streaks or yellow seams along the edges. Mountains, forests, caves, waterfalls, still waters. A cave turned violet. A sea of clouds as pink as a cheek. A field of snow in black and white. The frames remain empty, the tension rises. Charli Sas sums it up: “Some carry associations with death, demons, or otherworldly forces; others seem to reveal nothing.” Then, further on: “Yet once you have encountered the yōkai, that nothingness begins to feel inhabited.”

At Picto New York, the hanging takes the form of an emaki (絵巻), the Japanese illustrated handscroll unrolled with one hand and rolled up with the other, scene after scene. Yuji Watanabe had not planned it: the idea, the artist says, came later, when he was working out the exhibition space. A soundscape by Pinkcourtesyphone, the project of composer Richard Chartier, runs from one photograph to the next and extends the uncertainty beyond the image. The curator places the whole “somewhere between dream and nightmare.” Well measured.

Among the places photographed is Mount Osore, at the northern tip of Honshu, often described as a border between this world and the afterlife. Yuji Watanabe set down his camera there and left the frame empty, for the fallen gods to move in. “I took each and every photograph with a deep sense of gratitude.”

“Yōkai and Landscapes” by Yuji Watanabe is on view at Picto New York in Brooklyn through December 15, 2026.

article_text:
Ideas

From Property to Pixels: Shenzhen’s New Topography of Museums

Few cities have remade their cultural identity with the velocity of Shenzhen. Founded as a Special Economic Zone in 1980, the manufacturing hub has evolved into a tech powerhouse of 18 million residents with a median age of 32.5. 1 This youthful, domestic migrant demographic defines the local museum audience. Lacking existing institutional lineages, the city built its cultural topography within a single generation, shaped by municipal land allocation and shifting financial forces.

Shenzhen’s early contemporary art museum sector relied on real-estate patronage, with developers using cultural venues as placemaking assets to lift surrounding property values. Following the 2021–22 property market correction, this leveraged model gave way to a fragmented institutional landscape run by state enterprises, retail developers, and big tech. Over the past decade, roughly 34 art and design spaces launched across Shenzhen. 2 This expansion aligns with the cultural policy targets of China’s “14th Five‑Year Plan,” which position such institutions as a pillar of domestic soft power.

Launched in 2018, Shenzhen’s “Ten Cultural Facilities in the New Era” program anchors this shift by redirecting public financing away from property speculation toward civic institutions. Beneath this construction surge lies a deeper reconfiguration of patronage and governance. The city’s museums fall within four overlapping archetypes, each defined by evolving arrangements of land tenure, state oversight, and private capital. Together they trace a decisive break from property-driven space activations toward purpose-built infrastructure.

The first generation emerged as developer-funded civic amenities, epitomized by the OCT Contemporary Art Terminal (OCAT). Founded in 2005, OCAT set a local precedent by staging rigorous contemporary art exhibitions supported by the property profits of the OCT Group. By late 2022, however, OCAT’s programming shrank sharply following a broader nationwide contraction among institutions dependent on developer largesse and lacking independent endowments.

Well before this model faltered, a hybrid operating structure surfaced with the 2017 launch of the Sea World Culture and Arts Center (SWCAC). Sited on state land in Shekou but developed by China Merchants Shekou (CMSK), the center is operated by Design Society, a cultural initiative established by CMSK with London’s Victoria and Albert Museum as its founding partner. The arrangement pioneered a model that paired state-enterprise management with international museum expertise.

As CMSK’s inaugural contemporary art and design institution, the venue saw its governance evolve alongside its growth, transitioning to direct operation under China Merchants Culture Industry in 2020. It has largely pulled off this balancing act, sustaining credible, if pragmatic, contemporary art and design programming via retail partnerships, rentals, and ticketed shows. Periodically, its agenda also aligns with state priorities, including hosting the Shanhua Award traditional Chinese crafts showcase during the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Today, led by director Xijia Zhang, the center navigates the friction between curatorial autonomy, corporate mandates, and political expectations. As Zhang notes, “The real test for a cultural institution is not only surviving on its own ledger but sustaining the capacity to generate authentic cultural value within a commercial framework.” 3

SWCAC has shown that a state enterprise could run a serious cultural institution. This paved the way for a new cohort of state-owned venues marked by a striking step-change in architectural scale. The Shenzhen Bay Culture Square in Houhai opened in late 2025, followed by the Shenzhen International Museum of Art (SIMoA) in May 2026 in Guangming. Both were conceived under compressed timelines at “Shenzhen speed,” juggling large-scale construction with the rapid mobilization of curatorial teams ahead of their launches.

Sited on prime coastal parkland, the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square occupies a prominent civic position. Owned by the city government, the biomorphic complex designed by Ma Yansong’s MAD Architects is operated by China Resources Land under an asset-light management model separating land ownership from programming. Echoing SWCAC’s early strategy, it pairs a marquee building with a curatorial focus on design and architecture. Through multiyear agreements with institutions including Tate Modern and the London Design Museum, the venue taps into collection loans, co-curatorial expertise, and joint educational programs—project-based exchanges rather than the foundational operational consultancy the V&A once provided to SWCAC.

By contrast, SIMoA pulls the city’s institutional weight northward to Guangming Science City. As a district-government-led project built on reserved public land and operated by Poly Culture, the museum anchors a nascent cultural cluster far from Nanshan’s established epicenter. Reflecting this mandate, the museum’s inaugural Shenzhen Art and Technology Biennale aligns its program with Guangming’s state-designated identity as an innovation zone.

While outsourcing management to state-owned contractors insulates these mega-museums from real-estate volatility, operational pressures remain. Institutional KPIs often favor high-turnout, imported blockbusters over labor-intensive local commissions, a tension amplified by hyper-accelerated schedules from construction to opening.

Where the state seeks civic prestige, luxury retail looks for cultural differentiation. Operating as a for-profit cultural enterprise without a permanent collection, Fotografiska Shenzhen positions itself as a hospitality and lifestyle brand rather than a traditional collecting museum. Within the Shenzhen Bay MixC, China Resources supplies the commercial premises while Fotografiska runs the 5,300-square-meter venue, an arrangement that extends the “art-mall” model into a broader, district-level retail strategy.

Driven by real-estate logic, this partnership explores how to “use culture as an engine to reshape the value of commercial property,” as noted by Liu Jie, general manager of Shenzhen Bay MixC. 4 Applying lessons from its earlier Shanghai outpost, Fotografiska replaces the quiet white cube with a multilayered lifestyle destination. By blending photography and new media exhibitions with retail, a VIP lounge, and hospitality, it integrates curatorial prestige into the mall’s floor plan as a point of distinction. Structured to break even rather than generate profits, the space fulfills its retail-anchoring mandate. Having opened only in October 2026, however, its ability to sustain curatorial rigor over time remains untested.

Yet, if luxury retail seeks cultural differentiation for real estate, a distinct realignment occurs as patronage migrates from commercial spaces to virtual networks and hardware ecosystems. This change is embodied in two major projects under construction in Houhai. The Róng Museum, commissioned through Tencent founder Ma Huateng’s private venture Tenova Future, is slated for a 2027 opening within the M80 complex. Across the bay, the JD Museum is scheduled to open in late 2027 inside JD.com’s Scenic-City compound, fulfilling a planning requirement to allocate floor area to cultural use.

The Róng Museum’s Ole Scheeren-designed building intentionally blurs the boundaries between gallery spaces and the surrounding urban campus. Bringing 14 years of experience from Hong Kong’s M+ and Tai Kwun Contemporary, founding director Pi Li notes the distinct requirements of the city. “Shenzhen is a different city, with a different demographic structure, pace of development, and cultural ecology,” he states. “Rather than replicating the Hong Kong model, our task is to build an institution that is genuinely rooted in Shenzhen while remaining internationally connected.” 5

Pi Li frames the two cities as complementary cultural nodes: Hong Kong offers established institutional expertise and global networks, while Shenzhen provides experimental vitality. Guided by the concept of róng (integration or interconnectedness), the museum rejects overt corporate branding, positioning itself as a learning-centered platform spanning art, architecture, and performance. To cultivate a local audience, Pi Li emphasizes critical inquiry into technology’s impact on humanity over superficial digital spectacles, navigating the distinct tastes of cross-border visitors and local residents, while focusing on long-term commissions rather than rapid collection-building.

Nearby, the JD Museum is also designed by Scheeren, with interiors by Neri&Hu. The institution locates itself at the intersection of hardware-driven material production and creative thought. “There are conversations that can be had here that can’t be had anywhere else. . . . this is the place where materiality meets ideas, whether those ideas are in computer science and programming or the ideas within art and culture,” executive director Robin Peckham explains. 6

Peckham similarly distances the museum’s program from purely interactive digital formats, a position formalized in JD’s “Museum Manifesto”: the galleries “will never become product showcases, but host weirdness that complicates your idea of what technology is and what the lifestyle of the future might be.”

Ahead of its physical launch, the museum initiated “Unboxing JD Museum” to build familiarity with contemporary art and museum practices from the inside out. Reimagining JD’s iconic delivery boxes as mobile “Unboxing Pavilions” alongside workplace exhibitions and workshops, it engages JD’s 900,000-strong workforce and their families. Simultaneously, it collaborates with artists, curators, and architects through pop-up workshops and touring public projects at civic venues, translating professional peer dialogue into accessible programming. The museum’s layout includes the “Sanctuary and Cave Galleries” for immersive, site-specific commissions and performances, complemented by a 178-seat performance hall and learning labs. Though Róng and JD pursue independent curatorial agendas, their teams engage in practical cooperation, including jointly hosting international museum and patron delegations to raise the city’s profile.

As officials and business leaders gathered for the APEC summit in November 2026, SIMoA and Shenzhen Bay Culture Square welcomed these visiting dignitaries, placing this unfolding patronage experiment on the global stage. Beneath the showcase, fundamental operational questions persist. It remains to be seen how independent curators and local practitioners will gain visibility alongside these heavily resourced flagships, and whether these large institutions can sustainably serve Shenzhen’s residents as well as cross-border audiences.

Ultimately, the evolution of Shenzhen’s museum landscape marks a permanent shift away from real-estate patronage toward a complex matrix of state capital and policy mandates, commercial-lifestyle hybrids, and big tech capital. Land-use regulations, targeted operating subsidies, and corporate funding frameworks are shaping the characters of these institutions—who governs them, and where cultural experimentation can occur. Credible institutional standing, after all, is earned by cultivating public trust over time. The defining test for Shenzhen’s museum boom lies ahead: whether its expanding network of state and corporate-backed institutions can create a sustainable ecosystem for local artists, arts professionals, and the general public, rather than simply adding fancy monuments to the city’s skyline.

Patricia Li is a Hong Kong-based art and culture strategist, writer, and editor focusing on contemporary visual culture. Formerly with Art Basel, she has lived and worked across London, Tokyo, and New York. She holds an MA from Central Saint Martins and a BSc from the London School of Economics.

年にロンドンで初演され、作曲家ベンジャミン・ブリテンの名を一躍高めた代表作。一人の漁師と、彼を糾弾する共同体の緊張を描いた本作は、初演から 80 年以上を経た今の時代にも、鋭い問いを投げかけます。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "開幕に先立つ 11 月 21 日、ゲネプロを取材しました。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一人の漁師を追い詰める村人たち"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "物語の舞台は、 1830 年頃のイギリス東海岸にある漁村。徒弟の少年の死をめぐる審問を受けた漁師ピーター・グライムズは、「事故だった」と無実を訴えます。しかし、もともと村人たちから敬遠されていた彼に向けられるのは、疑惑と不信のまなざし。彼に寄り添うエレンの支えを得て新たな徒弟を迎えますが、その少年ジョンもまた不慮の死を遂げます。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "疑惑と敵意を募らせる村人たちに追い詰められ、グライムズは次第に逃げ場を失っていきます。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "終わらない裁き ―― カーセンの演出が描く孤独と集団心理"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "演出を手がけるのはロバート・カーセン。現在、世界的に最も評価の高いオペラ演出家のひとりといってよいでしょう。 2023 年のミラノ・スカラ座初演で絶賛された本プロダクションを東京で上演します。今回はカーセン本人が来日し、トークイベントにも参加するなど力が入っています。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/9d758408e6bc62d4c956f135a78ea316.jpg", "舞台は、木張りの壁に囲まれた閉鎖的な空間。村の集会所や法廷、パブ、グライムズの小屋へと姿を変えながらも、冒頭のベンチは終盤まで舞台に残ります。まるでグライムズに対する裁きが、物語の終わりまで続いているかのようです。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "スクリーンに映し出されるグライムズの表情からは、不安や恐怖が生々しく伝わってきます。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/5ff4600fa40ea821a8eda261bea34ff6.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "撮影：堀田力丸　提供：新国立劇場", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "舞台全体を一段上から取り囲むように設えられたスペースがあり、折々そこから芝居に絡む合唱も効果的です。村人たちの視線と声が、逃げ場のないグライムズを取り囲み、村全体が一つの大きな意思となって彼に迫ってきます。集団心理が音楽として立ち上がり、彼を追い詰めていく様はぞっとします。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "とりわけ印象的だったのが、村人たちがグライムズを探し、罪を追及しようと迫る場面です。手にしたライトの強烈な光が舞台上を走り、客席にまで向けられる。その冷たく、凶器のような光には恐怖心を覚えます。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/5570b50d105bce25721b18272b86c16d.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "撮影：堀田力丸　提供：新国立劇場", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ブリテンの音楽が描く深淵"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "オーケストラ作品としても広く親しまれている「 4 つの海の間奏曲」をはじめ、静かな海の表情から荒れ狂う嵐、月光に至るまで、自然の情景を雄弁に描き出すブリテンの音楽は秀逸です。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ブリテン作品を得意とする大野和士芸術監督の指揮のもと、東京フィルハーモニー交響楽団の緻密かつダイナミックな響きが、登場人物たちの不安や心の奥に潜む狂気まで浮かび上がらせています。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ジョヴァノヴィッチが演じるグライムズ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "スカラ座公演でも好評を博したテノール、ブランドン・ジョヴァノヴィッチの豊かな表現力が光ります。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/9995cd0c5f1daf5bcc3fa28721dd93d8.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "paragraph", "text": "星々が規則正しく巡る夜空と、混乱に満ちた人間世界の対比。その描写は美しくも、グライムズの孤独をいっそう際立たせるようでした。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「 In dreams I’ve built myself some kindlier home （夢に築いた優しい家）」と歌うように、無骨で激しい気性のグライムズの胸の内にも、家を持ち、家庭を築き、店を構え、エレンと結婚したいという穏やかな暮らしへの憧れがありました。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "誰もが正義を語る ―― 村人たちの複雑な人間模様"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
新国立劇場で 11 月 23 日（月・祝）、オペラ《ピーター・グライムズ》が開幕しました。

1945 年にロンドンで初演され、作曲家ベンジャミン・ブリテンの名を一躍高めた代表作。一人の漁師と、彼を糾弾する共同体の緊張を描いた本作は、初演から 80 年以上を経た今の時代にも、鋭い問いを投げかけます。

開幕に先立つ 11 月 21 日、ゲネプロを取材しました。

一人の漁師を追い詰める村人たち

物語の舞台は、 1830 年頃のイギリス東海岸にある漁村。徒弟の少年の死をめぐる審問を受けた漁師ピーター・グライムズは、「事故だった」と無実を訴えます。しかし、もともと村人たちから敬遠されていた彼に向けられるのは、疑惑と不信のまなざし。彼に寄り添うエレンの支えを得て新たな徒弟を迎えますが、その少年ジョンもまた不慮の死を遂げます。

疑惑と敵意を募らせる村人たちに追い詰められ、グライムズは次第に逃げ場を失っていきます。

終わらない裁き ―― カーセンの演出が描く孤独と集団心理

演出を手がけるのはロバート・カーセン。現在、世界的に最も評価の高いオペラ演出家のひとりといってよいでしょう。 2023 年のミラノ・スカラ座初演で絶賛された本プロダクションを東京で上演します。今回はカーセン本人が来日し、トークイベントにも参加するなど力が入っています。

舞台は、木張りの壁に囲まれた閉鎖的な空間。村の集会所や法廷、パブ、グライムズの小屋へと姿を変えながらも、冒頭のベンチは終盤まで舞台に残ります。まるでグライムズに対する裁きが、物語の終わりまで続いているかのようです。

スクリーンに映し出されるグライムズの表情からは、不安や恐怖が生々しく伝わってきます。

舞台全体を一段上から取り囲むように設えられたスペースがあり、折々そこから芝居に絡む合唱も効果的です。村人たちの視線と声が、逃げ場のないグライムズを取り囲み、村全体が一つの大きな意思となって彼に迫ってきます。集団心理が音楽として立ち上がり、彼を追い詰めていく様はぞっとします。

とりわけ印象的だったのが、村人たちがグライムズを探し、罪を追及しようと迫る場面です。手にしたライトの強烈な光が舞台上を走り、客席にまで向けられる。その冷たく、凶器のような光には恐怖心を覚えます。

ブリテンの音楽が描く深淵

オーケストラ作品としても広く親しまれている「 4 つの海の間奏曲」をはじめ、静かな海の表情から荒れ狂う嵐、月光に至るまで、自然の情景を雄弁に描き出すブリテンの音楽は秀逸です。

ブリテン作品を得意とする大野和士芸術監督の指揮のもと、東京フィルハーモニー交響楽団の緻密かつダイナミックな響きが、登場人物たちの不安や心の奥に潜む狂気まで浮かび上がらせています。

ジョヴァノヴィッチが演じるグライムズ

スカラ座公演でも好評を博したテノール、ブランドン・ジョヴァノヴィッチの豊かな表現力が光ります。

彼が歌う独白的なソロ「 Now the Great Bear and Pleiades （大熊座とプレアデス星団は）」では、澄んだ星空が静けさとともに目の前に広がるようでした。

星々が規則正しく巡る夜空と、混乱に満ちた人間世界の対比。その描写は美しくも、グライムズの孤独をいっそう際立たせるようでした。

「 In dreams I’ve built myself some kindlier home （夢に築いた優しい家）」と歌うように、無骨で激しい気性のグライムズの胸の内にも、家を持ち、家庭を築き、店を構え、エレンと結婚したいという穏やかな暮らしへの憧れがありました。

誰もが正義を語る ―― 村人たちの複雑な人間模様

ブリテンは、社会に溶け込めない人々や、弱者、疎外された人々への眼差しを持ち続けた作曲家です。同性愛者として生きた彼自身の経験も、その創作と無縁ではないでしょう。

物語の中心にいるのは、孤立した漁師グライムズだけではありません。ブリテンの鋭い観察眼が描き出す、ひとクセもふたクセもある登場人物たちを、実力派歌手たちが巧みに演じています。

彼を理解し、救おうとする未亡人の教師エレン・オーフォード（サリー・マシューズ）、人格者として彼を気にかける退役船長バルストロード（ジョーダン・シャナハン）。

一方、村人たちが集うパブ「ボーア亭」を切り盛りする女主人アーンティ（ニコール・ピッコロミーニ）と二人の姪（渡邊仁美、今野沙知恵）、敬虔なメソジストで短気な漁師ボブ・ボウルズ（糸賀修平）、法律家で検死官も務める村長スワロー（河野鉄平）など、村にはさまざまな立場や価値観を持つ人々が暮らしています。

なかでも、噂話と詮索が大好きで、グライムズが少年を殺したと信じて疑わないセドリー夫人（齊藤純子）の存在は強烈。ほかにも、村の牧師ホレース・アダムス（村上公太）、薬屋ネッド・キーン（吉川健一）、荷車引きのホブソン（大塚博章）らが登場し、小さな漁村の共同体を形づくっています。

彼らもまた、それぞれの個性と矛盾を抱えた存在として描かれています。

特に興味深いのは、女性たちの描かれ方です。エレンにはどことなく、家庭的な優しさや母性といった役割を期待するような視線が向けられます。そんなエレンを演じるサリー・マシューズの、柔らかさと芯の強さを併せ持つ歌唱も魅力的でした。

また、パブの女性たちが「私たちは笑うべきか、泣くべきか」と歌う場面には、彼女たちの嘆きや諦めがにじむようでした。活気あふれる営業中のパブと掃除の時間に漂う日常の空気。その対比には、どこか物悲しい余韻がありました。

現代社会にもいる？ スワローとセドリー夫人

なかでも、現代でも出会えそうな人物として異彩を放っていたのが、スワローとセドリー夫人でした。どちらも自分なりの理屈を持ち、村の人間関係のなかで巧みに立ち回っているように見えてきます。

弁護士であり村長、検死官も務めるスワロー（河野鉄平）は、自分の立場や体面を守るため、周囲の目を巧みに意識しながら立ち回る人物です。一見信頼できそうな外見でありながら、腹の内を見せない人物像がよく表れていました。

一方、噂話やスキャンダルを好み、他人の不幸さえ自分の好奇心や正義感の材料にしてしまう裕福な未亡人、セドリー夫人（齊藤純子）。立ち聞きした断片的な話を、いつの間にか確信に変えて人に伝えていく。正義を掲げることが、自己を支える使命感になっているようにも見える興味深い人物像でした。

噂話や他人の不幸にさえ刺激を求めるその姿は、SNSやショート動画に踊らされる現代のドーパミン中毒者のようでもあります。

噂がつくり上げる虚像、繰り返される悲劇

噂はいつしか実像を覆い、ひとりの人間を別の姿につくり変えてしまいます。村人たちが見ているのは、目の前のグライムズではなく、噂がつくり上げた虚像なのかもしれません。

追い詰められ、静かに海の底へと沈んでいくグライムズは、まるで、人々が抱える恐怖や不安を一身に引き受けて逝ったかのようでもありました。

「陸が見えなくなるまで沖へ出て、船を沈めるように」。それは彼を支えてきたバルストロードが指示したことでもあったのです。

救いを求めながら、誰かを傷つける男

グライムズは村人たちから疎外され、偏見や疑惑にさらされる一方、自らも周囲との関係を築けず、差し伸べられた手も拒んでしまいます。

少年を手荒に鍛えようとしながら、適切な導き方も愛情の伝え方も知らない。村人たちに認められたい、穏やかな家庭を築きたい。そんな願いを抱きながらも、彼はその思いを他者との関係のなかで実現することができません。

グライムズは社会に追い詰められた犠牲者なのか。それとも、自らの行動によって破滅を招いたのか。彼の孤独に心を寄せるほど、その境界は曖昧になっていきます。

芸術は、社会の矛盾を映し出す

既存の社会システムだけでは答えの出ない問いに向き合い、人間や共同体の本質を照らし出す。それもまた、芸術の持つ力です。

ブリテン没後 50 年の節目に上演される《ピーター・グライムズ》。今なお私たちの社会に鋭い問いを投げかける本作を、ぜひ劇場でご体感ください。（ライター・山本まりこ）

article_text:
“ Clayface ,” a body-horror film based on a little-known comic book, opened to $24 million, a middling result for DC Studios, which is in year two of its mixed-bag theatrical revival.

On the one hand, the gross isn’t bad considering that the title character is a niche player and the gory genre isn’t associated with the spandex set. On the other, it’s slightly below projections, which predicted that “Clayface” would open to between $25 million to $30 million. It was enough to hold off the second weekend of A24’s “You Can See Everything,” which earned $19.5 million. It also helps that “Clayface” is cheaper than most comic book movies, carrying a price tag of $44 million. It may not be a profit-generating machine, but it won’t lose money either.

That wasn’t the case with “Supergirl,” the previous film in the universe that James Gunn and Peter Safran have been building since they took the reins at DC. “Supergirl” was a disaster, losing an estimated $80 million to $120 million . It also received a critical drubbing. “Clayface” fared better in that respect too. It stands at 75% “fresh” on Rotten Tomatoes compared to “Supergirl’s” 52% “rotten” rating. So far, last summer’s “Superman,” which Gunn wrote and directed, is the most successful example of their quippy, poppy approach. It earned $618.7 million globally and was widely embraced by critics. The company’s streaming shows, which include “Lanterns” and “Peacemaker,” have been better received.

But nothing DC has produced under Gunn and Safran has come close to the box office heights enjoyed by Christopher Nolan’s “The Dark Knight” trilogy, the first “Aquaman,” or “Wonder Woman.” Two of Nolan’s “Dark Knight” movies topped $1 billion, as did “Aquaman,” while “Wonder Woman” earned $823.9 million. When Gunn and Safran were enlisted to revitalize DC, the brand was struggling with consistency, with films like “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom” and “The Flash” collapsing in spectacular fashion — they were little seen and little enjoyed. The product the pair has produced has improved on that low bar, even as DC’s more recent efforts have yet to deliver the same gloriously demented pleasures of Gunn’s “Guardians of the Galaxy” films. Safran, a veteran producer whose credits include “The Conjuring” franchise, is seen as the business brains of the operation, while Gunn speaks comic book and is tasked with charting the creative vision.

Looking ahead, DC will bring back some of its headliners. “The Batman: Part II” will open in theaters in 2028, while Gunn will return to the world of Superman with next summer’s “Man of Tomorrow.” Both films seem poised to connect with audiences.

Ultimately, Gunn and Safran may just have the misfortune of leading a comic book empire at a time when audiences are getting much more selective about their costumed heroes. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is the highest-grossing film of the year, having earned $2.5 billion, but that film features one of the most iconic comic book characters in history. Likewise, “Avengers: Doomsday” is expected to be a blockbuster when it opens in December, but it boasts Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans returning to the MCU. Outside of those Tiffany brands, even Marvel, which DC so clearly wants to emulate, has struggled. The company’s attempts to build up a new group of Avengers, such as “Thunderbolts,” “The Fantastic Four: First Steps,” “The Eternals,” and “The Marvels,” have been box office disappointments, if not outright bombs . If the king of comic book universes is struggling, maybe it’s wrong to hope for more from Gunn and Safran. In that kind of atmosphere, “Clayface” may count as a win, modest though its victory may be.

title_original: Musei e uffici del MiC, il nodo Ales e il futuro di 2500 lavoratori della cultura
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "La data del 31 dicembre 2027 pesa sul futuro di oltre 2500 lavoratrici e lavoratori, impiegati nei musei, nei parchi archeologici, negli archivi, nelle biblioteche e negli uffici del Ministero della Cultura: è il termine fissato dall’attuale quadro normativo per l’utilizzo di Ales – Arte Lavoro e Servizi Spa , società in house del MiC che negli ultimi anni ha assunto un ruolo sempre più esteso nel funzionamento della rete culturale statale.", "links": [{"text": "Ales – Arte Lavoro e Servizi Spa", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/ales/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A lanciare nuovamente l’allarme sono Filcams Cgil, Fisascat Cisl e UilTucs, che chiedono al ministro della Cultura Alessandro Giuli la convocazione urgente di un tavolo istituzionale. article_text:
La data del 31 dicembre 2027 pesa sul futuro di oltre 2500 lavoratrici e lavoratori, impiegati nei musei, nei parchi archeologici, negli archivi, nelle biblioteche e negli uffici del Ministero della Cultura: è il termine fissato dall’attuale quadro normativo per l’utilizzo di Ales – Arte Lavoro e Servizi Spa , società in house del MiC che negli ultimi anni ha assunto un ruolo sempre più esteso nel funzionamento della rete culturale statale.

A lanciare nuovamente l’allarme sono Filcams Cgil, Fisascat Cisl e UilTucs, che chiedono al ministro della Cultura Alessandro Giuli la convocazione urgente di un tavolo istituzionale. Secondo i sindacati, il tempo a disposizione è ormai breve, perché per garantire continuità alla società e salvaguardare l’occupazione sarebbe necessario un intervento normativo. In assenza di risposte, le tre sigle hanno annunciato una campagna straordinaria di assemblee nei luoghi di lavoro, destinata a culminare in un’assemblea nazionale a Roma, senza escludere successive mobilitazioni.

Ales, perché il 31 dicembre 2027 è una data decisiva per i lavoratori della cultura

Il nodo deriva dall’articolo 1-ter del decreto-legge 104 del 2019, modificato negli anni successivi. La disposizione autorizza il Ministero della Cultura ad avvalersi di Ales per attività di accoglienza e vigilanza nei musei e nei parchi archeologici, oltre che per servizi di supporto tecnico, amministrativo e contabile, nelle more delle procedure concorsuali necessarie a soddisfare il fabbisogno di personale del dicastero e comunque non oltre il 31 dicembre 2027.

Tale formulazione lega il futuro di Ales al progressivo completamento degli organici ministeriali. In altre parole, la società è stata utilizzata anche come risposta alla cronica carenza di personale del MiC, mentre parallelamente lo Stato procedeva – con tempi spesso molto più lunghi – alle assunzioni tramite concorso.

Negli ultimi anni i diversi concorsi per funzionari, assistenti e altre figure professionali hanno effettivamente cercato di ricostituire gli organici del Ministero. Questo processo riduce almeno in parte il peso che Ales ha avuto negli anni più difficili della carenza di personale ma apre una questione occupazionale: più le strutture ministeriali vengono rifornite di personale pubblico, più diventa necessario definire quali funzioni debbano continuare a essere affidate alla partecipata e quale destino debbano avere le professionalità – in molti casi altamente specializzate – già impiegate.

Una società diventata strutturale per musei e uffici

Fondata nel 1998, interamente partecipata dal Ministero della Cultura dal 2009 e attualmente guidata dal presidente e amministratore delegato Fabio Tagliaferri , Ales è cresciuta fino a diventare una delle strutture più rilevanti nel funzionamento operativo del sistema culturale statale. La legge le attribuisce attività di supporto alla conservazione e alla valorizzazione del patrimonio, all’accoglienza e alla vigilanza, oltre a funzioni tecnico-amministrative. Il Ministero può inoltre avvalersene per gli interventi connessi al PNRR, in questo caso fino alla conclusione del Piano e comunque entro il 31 dicembre 2026.

Secondo le organizzazioni sindacali, oggi Ales conta oltre 2.500 dipendenti. È una dimensione che rende difficile considerare la vicenda come una normale riorganizzazione aziendale: negli anni la società ha di fatto sostenuto una parte molto ampia della rete museale e degli uffici culturali italiani, compensando vuoti di organico che in alcuni casi incidevano direttamente sulla possibilità di garantire aperture, servizi al pubblico e attività amministrative.

Una cessazione improvvisa o una forte riduzione delle attività, senza un piano di transizione, potrebbe quindi produrre conseguenze sia sui posti di lavoro che sulla continuità di moltissimi servizi. Il rischio di una paralisi generalizzata va valutato alla luce del progressivo ingresso di nuovo personale ministeriale ma rimane evidente la necessità di capire quali attività oggi dipendano ancora concretamente dai lavoratori Ales e quali possano essere assorbite dagli organici pubblici.

Il confronto con l’azienda e le incognite sul futuro

Nell’incontro del 3 novembre, secondo quanto riferito dai sindacati, il management di Ales ha ribadito la solidità economica della società e la volontà di lavorare per superare il limite temporale previsto dalla normativa, anche individuando nuovi servizi specialistici da svolgere a supporto del Ministero. Non sono però emerse garanzie definitive sul futuro dell’azienda e dei suoi dipendenti.

Già nelle scorso settimane, UilTucs aveva richiamato l’attenzione sull’Atto di indirizzo del Ministero della Cultura del 25 agosto 2026, che contiene indicazioni su riorganizzazione, nuove attività, politiche del personale, formazione, riqualificazione, rapporti a tempo determinato e interventi collegati al PNRR. Il sindacato aveva però espresso dubbi sulle modalità concrete di applicazione, soprattutto rispetto alla possibile riallocazione del personale tra commesse e alla varietà delle professionalità presenti nella società.

Per Filcams, Fisascat e UilTucs la questione non può quindi essere risolta esclusivamente all’interno del rapporto tra management e lavoratori. La richiesta è che il confronto venga trasferito sul piano politico, perché l’eventuale prosecuzione delle attività oltre il 2027 richiede una scelta normativa. I sindacati chiedono che la discussione inizi ora. «Non chiediamo rassicurazioni generiche», affermano, ma un confronto istituzionale sul futuro della società e dell’occupazione.

Ales e l’ibridazione tra pubblico e privato nella cultura

La vicenda riapre anche una questione più generale sul modello con cui negli ultimi anni è stato organizzato il lavoro nel settore culturale pubblico. Pur essendo una società interamente controllata dal Ministero, Ales assume i propri dipendenti con contratti di natura privatistica e rappresenta forse l’esempio più evidente di quella zona di confine tra pubblico e privato che si è progressivamente ampliata anche nella gestione dei beni culturali italiani.

Il modello ha consentito al Ministero di reclutare personale con maggiore rapidità rispetto ai tempi dei concorsi pubblici e di rispondere a carenze diventate strutturali. Allo stesso tempo, però, ha prodotto una condizione più vulnerabile per migliaia di lavoratori che svolgono attività di interesse pubblico senza appartenere direttamente ai ruoli ministeriali.

A questa ambiguità si aggiunge un secondo problema, emerso più volte nell’organizzazione concreta del lavoro: il rapporto non sempre lineare tra competenze possedute, mansioni, inquadramenti e destinazioni operative. La flessibilità che ha reso Ales uno strumento utile per tamponare rapidamente le necessità del sistema può diventare, quando mutano le esigenze del Ministero, uno degli elementi di maggiore fragilità.

article_text:
Interview

How Miles Greenberg Got “WAR” Past the Censors

“There was not a single outlet, institution, or gallery that wanted to get behind this thing,” the artist told Hyperallergic about his new, six-hour performance piece.

Miles Greenberg’s mother took him to see Marina Abramović perform The Artist Is Present at the Museum of Modern Art when he was just 12 years old. The experience would serve as the zero point for the New York-based Canadian artist’s own performance-based practice, and the birth of his unyielding desire to “see [his] work at a museum, where it would be approached as a sculpture.” Later training under playwright Robert Wilson, choreographer Édouard Lock, and the very “grandmother of performance art” who spurred his interest in the medium, Greenberg began developing works that ironically share more with the histories of painting and sculpture than a lineage of performance. He has stood on plinths as the tortured satyr Marsyas from Greek mythology, the arrow-pierced Christian martyr Saint Sebastian, and in original statuesque poses that recall the Baroque ecstasy of a Bernini sculpture.

On October 29, the artist presented “WAR” (2026), a six-hour durational performance organized by Performa and curated by Zoe Lukov. More than 40 performers walked on treadmills in the vacant site of the former 86th Street Cinema in New York to a trance-like score by artist Chino Amobi. Greenberg spoke with Hyperallergic about the difficulties of securing a venue for the work amid Israel's genocide on Palestine, the limitations of endurance, and performance as a “gateway into a state that is difficult to reach.”

Hyperallergic: You often reference martyrs, saints, warriors, and other archetypes across history dedicated to either heroic causes or beliefs beyond themselves. Why are you interested in these figures? Do they resonate with you besides their art-historical or imagistic qualities?

Miles Greenberg: The West has canonized these stories as a means of cutting right to a series of moralistic teachings that have been central to Western societies writ large for the last several millennia. They're represented in different ways, but there's this longstanding tradition of just about every artist from the Renaissance up until contemporary times — though, maybe to a lesser extent — regurgitating these art-historical figures, characters, stories, and fables over and over again.

With performance, which continues to be niche and sit around the edges of art history, people’s minds go more to the shock value of it, which I’m not particularly seduced or interested by, rather than what it is that we mean or wish to convey. So it’s really a strategic play on my behalf to choreograph or rein in their imagination and channel it in the right direction. I think of these works as portraits more than I wish to identify with the figures. There can be some crossover. Saint Sebastian is a notable example I have some personal investment in as a queer person.

I also think situating myself centrally in that tradition helps to quite simply attribute value and clarity and define my practice within that canon and lineage of art history, rather than somehow adjacent or parallel to it as a young queer Black performance-based person. I’m not interested in marginality as a destination, and I don’t see any reason not to put me in conversation with the canon. I was raised by the canon, so I’m going to make like the canon.

H: What led you to turn to the subject of war with this particular work?

article_text:
After dozens of artists at the 61st Venice Biennale withdrew from award consideration in solidarity with the jury, which planned to omit Russia and Israel from the prizes and later resigned, the festival has announced Chicago-based artist Nick Cave and India's national pavilion as winners of its new visitors’ awards.

Nine days before the Venice Biennale opened on May 9, the women-led awards jury resigned en masse, shortly after announcing that countries facing accusations of crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court, notably Israel and Russia, would not be eligible for prizes.

The Biennale reversed the decision soon after the jury's resignation and replaced the traditional jury-selected Golden and Silver Lion awards with the “ Visitors' Lions ,” voted on by ticket-holders and awarded to the most popular pavilion and artist.
excerpt_original: The festival replaced its Golden Lions with new public-decided “Visitors’ Lions” after its jury resigned en masse in the fallout of a decision to exclude Israel and Russia from prizes.

article_text:
Art Basel Paris wegen Unruhen möglicherweise nicht das ganze Wochenende geöffnet, Kulturkampf in Kolumbien – und gehypte Doku über Elizabeth Holmes kommt nach Deutschland: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Donnerstag

Kunstmarkt

Roxana Azimi berichtet in "Le Monde" , dass die Spannungen in der Stadt den Andrang internationaler Sammler auf die Art Basel Paris nicht gebremst hätten. Die Messe überzeuge mit hochkarätigen Entdeckungen und politisch aufgeladenen Werken, etwa von Steven Parrino und Anita Molinero. Galeristen wie Georges-Philippe Vallois zeigten sich erleichtert: "Ich hatte befürchtet, dass der Kontext die Käufer abschrecken würde, aber das war nicht der Fall." Nathalie Obadia meldete mehr als 20 Verkäufe am ersten Nachmittag, Iwan Wirth lobte die "Widerstandsfähigkeit des Marktes". Zugleich beobachtet Azimi eine zunehmende Polarisierung: Während die Kunstwelt unter dem Eindruck der Proteste feiere, riefen radikale Stimmen zur Besetzung des Grand Palais auf. Händler Christian Berst warnt vor den Folgen für ein ganzes Ökosystem, das vom Kunstmarkt lebe. Ob die Messe wie geplant bis Sonntag geöffnet bleibt, ist offen. Ist Kunst ein Vebraucherthema? Zumindest kann es das sein. Im Magazin "Marktplatz" des Deutschlandfunks, das sich sonst eher um Stromverträge und Lebensmittelqualität dreht, ging es am heutigen Donnerstag um den Kauf von Kunst . Wie sich Anfängerinnen und Anfänger an dieses Feld herantrauen können, erklärten dabei unter anderem der Galerist Kristian Jarmuschek und der Kunstkritiker Stefan Koldehoff. Fazit: Keine Berührungsängste haben, Institutionen wie Galerien und Kunstvereine besuchen, viel fragen und nur kaufen, was man auch wirklich mag. Das mit der Geldanlage funktioniert eh nur sehr selten und mit sehr viel Expertise. Der Kunstmarkt, so entfesselt er manchmal sein mag, birgt immer noch einen großen Teil Unsicherheit und Zufall.

Kulturpolitik

Patricia Hempel beschäftigt sich in der "Berliner Zeitung" eingehender mit Wolfram Weimers Warnung vor einer möglichen rot-grün-roten Landesregierung in Berlin . Der Kulturstaatsminister drohte mit "direkten Auswirkungen auf die schwarz-rote Kulturpolitik im Bund". Das Bundesfinanzministerium stellt jedoch klar, dass der Hauptstadtfinanzierungsvertrag über rund fünf Milliarden Euro für 2028 bis 2037 rechtsverbindlich ist und keine Kündigungsmöglichkeit enthält. Offen bleibt, ob Weimer Fördermittel außerhalb des Vertrags antasten könnte. Die Berliner Grünen weisen seine Drohungen zurück. Landeschef Philmon Ghirmai empfiehlt ihm, "vor der eigenen Haustüre zu kehren", und verweist auf mögliche Kooperationen von CDU und AfD. Hempel zeigt, dass die konkreten Folgen von Weimers Warnung bislang ungeklärt sind.

Kim Córdova berichtet in "Artnet News" über einen politischen Eingriff in das Museo Nacional de Colombia in Bogotá . Nach der Ausrufung eines "Kulturkampf" durch den neuen kolumbianischen Präsidenten Abelardo de la Espriella ließ die Regierung Dutzende Kunstwerke und historische Objekte entfernen, darunter Zeugnisse des Friedensprozesses von 2016 sowie Arbeiten zu LGBTQ-Rechten und indigenen Gemeinschaften. Die Künstlerin Doris Salcedo nennt das Vorgehen wie "aus einer Anleitung für Nazis". Kritiker sehen darin einen Angriff auf die kulturelle Vielfalt und die Verfassung, die den Schutz des kulturellen Erbes garantiert. Am Montag ordnete ein Richter an, weitere Ausstellungsänderungen auszusetzen. Córdova stellt den Vorgang in den Kontext von Budgetkürzungen und dem Abbau staatlicher Kulturförderung. Künstler und Wissenschaftler reagieren mit Protesten und öffentlichen Lehrveranstaltungen vor dem Museum.

Die besondere Doku

Die überraschend erfolgreiche Dokumentation über die inhaftierte Theranos-Gründerin Elizabeth Holmes kommt in deutsche Kinos. Der Film "You Can See Everything" von Nathan Fielder und Lance Oppenheim startet hierzulande am 3. Dezember, wie Sony Pictures bei Instagram mitteilte. Zuvor hatte es Spekulationen gegeben, ob und wann die gehypte Doku, die bereits unzählige Memes generiert hat, nach ihrem US-Kinostart auch nach Deutschland kommt. In den USA läuft der Film bereits seit Mitte Oktober. Am ersten Wochenende spielte er 15 Millionen US-Dollar in 855 Kinos ein, wie aus Zahlen des Branchenportals "Boxoffice Mojo" hervorgeht. Das sei der beste Dokumentarfilmstart in Nordamerika ohne Konzertfilme seit mehr als 20 Jahren, berichteten mehrere US-Medien übereinstimmend. Einige Medien sehen "You Can See Everything" bereits als Oscar-Anwärter. Die Kritiken fallen auffallend positiv aus. Auf den Plattformen IMDb und Letterboxd, wo Nutzerinnen und Nutzer selbst Bewertungen abgeben, gehört die Doku bislang zu den am besten bewerteten Filmen überhaupt. Holmes war Gründerin und Chefin des Start-ups Theranos, mit dem sie Bluttests zu revolutionieren versprach. Bei Theranos reichten angeblich nur wenige Tropfen Blut auch für komplexe Tests. Holmes wurde gefeiert, Theranos erreichte in Finanzierungsrunden eine Bewertung von neun Milliarden Dollar. Holmes wurde damit auf dem Papier zur Milliardärin. Doch dann stellte sich heraus, dass die Technologie nicht funktionierte. Holmes und ihr Top-Manager Ramesh Balwani wurden wegen des Vorwurfs verurteilt, Investoren gezielt hinters Licht geführt zu haben. Sie ging 2023 ins Gefängnis. Nach aktuellen Angaben der US-Gefängnisverwaltung soll sie Ende Februar 2030 entlassen werden. Die Doku beginnt einen Monat vor dem Haftantritt. Nach der Premiere auf einem Filmfestival in den USA und dem starken Kinostart wurde in sozialen Medien auch die Frage über einen Kinostart in Deutschland immer lauter. Da ein genauer Termin lange offen geblieben war, kündigten manche Nutzer gar an, eine Reise über die Grenze nach Polen zu planen – dort soll der Film bereits am 6. November in die Kinos kommen. Den deutschen Starttermin kündigten mehrere Kinoketten nun ebenfalls direkt in sozialen Medien an und stießen damit auf großen Anklang.

article_text:
At The Photographers’ Gallery in London, ‘Sanlé Sory: Colour Years’ reveals a lesser-known chapter in the Burkinabé photographer’s career, documenting changing identities, cultural expression and everyday life in post-independence Burkina Faso.

What can a portrait reveal about a society in transformation? In ‘Sanlé Sory: Colour Years’, The Photographers’ Gallery revisits the remarkable career of one of West Africa’s most prolific photographers, revealing how colour photography captured the evolving identities and aspirations of a generation.

Best known for his black-and-white portraits of Bobo-Dioulasso’s vibrant youth culture, Sanlé Sory began experimenting with colour photography in the mid-1980s at his Volta Photo studio.

The exhibition presents meticulously restored colour prints from his archive, alongside record covers featuring Volta Jazz, a band associated with Burkina Faso’s flourishing post-independence music scene.

From families and couples to traders and shopkeepers, Sory’s portraits document changing fashions, relationships, and everyday experiences in a society negotiating political transformation and cultural exchange.

Established in 1960, the year of Upper Volta’s independence, Volta Photo became a space where individuals could construct and express their identities in front of the camera.

Curated by Taous Dahmani, ‘Colour Years’ offers a perspective on Sory’s enduring photographic legacy, foregrounding the relationship between portraiture, self-representation and social change.

Through colour, fashion and personal expression, the exhibition celebrates the individuals who shaped the visual history of modern Burkina Faso.

This exhibition is on view at The Photographers’ Gallery in London until 21 February 2027.

article_text:
T he Bloomsbury Group once induced yawns as the smug epitome of a snobbish high culture but they’re now admired for their feminism and queer abandon. There’s a West End play about the loves of the Bloomsbury economist John Maynard Keynes and if you visit the National Trust’s Sissinghurst , its flowerbeds are set alight by Vita Sackville-West’s affair with Virginia Woolf.

But biography can’t set art alight, as Tate Britain’s epic yet flaccid roam through the complicated lives and desperately mediocre paintings of the co-habiting Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant proves. While Keynes was quite the economist and Woolf a literary genius, I honestly can’t see enough interest in the visual art of Bloomsbury to detain anyone for long. That was true when their sex lives were spoken of in a more muted way (I read a biography of Keynes as a student and don’t remember any hanky-panky at all) and it’s true now, even as we trawl their paintings for gay and feminist meanings.

One caption for a male nude by Duncan Grant is so preoccupied with the erotic undertones, it says nothing about what is surely most interesting about the naked young man sitting on a table – that he is the same George Mallory who would vanish trying to climb Everest in 1924 and whose frozen body would be rediscovered there in 1999.

Perhaps the Himalaya is too wild to be encompassed in the sophisticated yet genteel world of Bloomsbury. Then again, so is Paris, in this exhibition. There is no French art here even though both Bell and Grant emulated French modernism, sometimes very belatedly. Grant’s portrait of Mallory, for instance, which dates from 1913, assiduously apes the style of Georges Seurat, who died in 1891.

In the early 1900s, almost every country in continental Europe was throwing up revolutionary modernist geniuses from Munch to Malevich , Schiele to Boccioni, but Britain was so visually repressed that the Bloomsbury Group seemed frightfully clever to have heard of modern art at all. It would have been more honest and interesting to show how this happened. Bell and Grant didn’t just see “post-impressionist” art, as their friend Roger Fry dubbed it, in exhibitions or magazines: they lived with it intimately. In 1918, Keynes famously hid a Cézanne still life of seven apples in a hedge near Bell and Grant’s place in the country, Charleston, because he couldn’t drive it up a muddy lane. When he got it to the house, the group all loved it.

Cézanne’s painting is a compacted philosophical masterpiece, which the Bloomsbury Group were right to admire, but it’s not here. Nor is the early cubist still life by Picasso, Pots and Lemon, that Vanessa’s art critic husband Clive Bell bought in 1911. Their inclusion would have given more context, and certainly more artistic excitement, to this show.

after newsletter promotion

Instead in a section on “modernisms” (what modernisms? There was only one modernism in the early 20th century) it feels as if the wool is being pulled over our eyes. We are supposed to believe that when Grant painted Head of Eve in 1913, a simplified totemic nude like a wooden carving, he was doing something utterly original rather than catching up with Picasso’s African-inspired fetishes, or that when Bell painted her wanly cubistic Portrait of Molly MacCarthy, she was in no way influenced by having a Picasso in the house.

The problem isn’t that Bell and Grant are playing catchup with Paris. It’s that both artists appear so detached and passionless. They try on avant garde ideas but always come back to tradition. Grant’s 1920s views of the South of France have a veneer of modern style but are the kind of holiday art a Victorian painter such as Lord Leighton might have done.

Sophistication and knowledge don’t guarantee greatness, nor does having an interesting life. Tate Britain probably wouldn’t put on a show by artists who were wife and husband but Vanessa and Duncan had a unique lifelong relationship even though he was gay and she married Clive Bell with whom she had children. But the pair don’t seem to influence or rival each other in a way to make a joint show come alive: indeed they cancel each other out. The pull of queer desire that’s a recurring impulse in Grant distracts you from the quiet still observations of Bell. Here is a openly sexed portrait by Grant of his lover David Garnett, over there a painting by Bell of her sister Woolf looking melancholically introspective.

In the Britain of their day, art was barely considered a serious pursuit and, for all their knowledge of French modernism, Bell and Grant are timid about how much any of this playing with brushes matters. But then you go into a little room near the end and find something with real belief: Grant’s erotic drawings. They are totally uninhibited, explicit and beautiful. His classical yet raw depictions of men having sex are like a queer version of Picasso’s Vollard Suite and for once the influence is digested in a creative, powerful way.

It’s the only time in this show that either artist seems truly driven. The rest is the stuff of Bloomsbury costume dramas.

article_text:
Although James Gunn ‘s journey with the Man of Steel has come to a close, Chris Pratt hopes they can take another adventure with Star-Lord soon.

The Guardians of the Galaxy star recently confessed he “would love” to make a fourth movie in the MCU franchise with Gunn, following his and Peter Safran’s departure from DC Studios amid David Ellison’s Skydance regime change.

“That would be awesome. I love working with James,” he told MovieZine . “He’s the man. I haven’t had the chance to speak with him since that news came out. But it’s interesting because anytime something like this comes up and you say it, it could always become a headline.”

Related Stories

DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In

Departing DC Co-Head James Gunn Reflects On “Trying” Four Years, Juggling Being Filmmaker & Exec

Pratt added, “All I’ll say is, I love James. He directed all three, and that’s pretty rare in those types of trilogies to have the same director through all three. So, if he wanted to come back and bring it back, man, I would just love that.”

Watch on Deadline

Earlier this week, Deadline reported that Gunn and Safran were out as co-CEOs and Chairmen of DC Studios after four years, but will continue to produce various DC projects. Meanwhile, Marvel’s former SVP of production and development, Jeremy Latcham, has been named DC’s new president and chief creative officer under Skydance’s takeover.

View this post on Instagram

Before stepping into his position as co-head of WBD’s newly formed DC Studios with Peter Safran in 2022, Gunn directed Guardians of the Galaxy (2014), Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (2017) and Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 (2023), as well as 2022’s The Guardian of the Galaxy Holiday Special , for Disney’s Marvel Studios .

article_text:
Candle Media cofounder Kevin Mayer told an industry conference in Doha on Friday that he had not foreseen the impending contraction in demand for streaming content in 2023, ahead of the company’s launch in 2021.

He was speaking six weeks after Candle Media hit the trade headlines for its sale of Reece Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine to Paris-based European content group Mediawan.

Candle Media originally acquired the company, behind Big Little Lies and The Morning Show , in 2021, as one of its first acquisitions for $900M. The re-sale price was not made public, but sources told Deadline that it was likely several hundreds of millions of dollars less than the original price.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic - Doha Industry Days

'Al Hayba' Star Taim Hasan To Play Syrian Whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan In Neon-Backed 'Caesar' Biopic

Mayer, who was talking to the Qatar Film Committee’s Industry Days event in Doha via video-link from L.A., did not dwell on the sale.

“On the live action side, we gave it a really good shot with Hello Sunshine and other assets. It was okay, but they didn’t work out to what we wanted, so we recently sold those,” he said.

Mayer did not go into details on why Hello Sunshine had not worked out for Candle Media, and there were no opportunities for questions from the floor.

His wider discussion, however, gave insight into some of the challenges facing the company as well as its triumphs led by its acquisition of Moonbug Entertainment, the children’s media company behind shows such as CoComelon , Blippi and Little Angel .

The former Disney exec, who oversaw the studio’s 2019 acquisition of 20th Century Fox and also helped spearhead the creation of Disney+ alongside Bon Iger, said the idea for Candle Media had been sparked by the studios getting into streaming and taking their IP in-house.

This trend, he said, suggested that streamers without big inhouse production capacity would be on the hunt for high-quality content.

“We felt that the value of being independent in that sort of industry, that vertically integrated, would be increasing, and I think that is still true. Being independent and having that that ability to sell to any of the streaming services is great,” he said.

“We also thought content demand would continue to increase double digits a year… with increasing demand globally for high-quality content, like we were producing at Candle Media, which would provide us with the volume we needed to make all of our acquisitions work financially,” he continued.

“Starting in 2023, that didn’t happen. In fact, the demand for streaming content actually contracted quite a bit, to about 35% below the peak of 2022. So, that part of our thesis was incorrect, unfortunately. We didn’t see that contraction coming.”

The second premise on which the company was built, he said, was the belief that strong IP and stories could exist on multiple formats.

“They could exist on YouTube and on TikTok and on other platforms as short form entertainment… they could coexist in traditional film, on streaming and television and elsewhere,” he said. “Then they would open up other revenue platforms such as consumer products licensing, which we did a lot with Disney, games, music…”

Mayer pointed to children’s media company Moonbug, which Candle Media acquired in 2021, as having fulfilled that goal thanks to shows like CoCocomelon , which was born on YouTube, and then repackaged for Netflix.

“We took those stories that came from YouTube, put them into one-hour compilations and licensed them to Netflix from 2021 to 2024. While CoComelon was the largest YouTube channel in the world, it was also the most popular Netflix show in the world. For three solid years, it was the number one streaming show and the number one YouTube show,” he said.

He said the operation had not worked in the opposite direction for more traditional IP.

“We were hopeful that we could take traditional film and TV and cross it over into social media. That didn’t work all that well. But what did work really well is taking social media storytelling and crossing it over to traditional. And you’ve seen Obsession and Backrooms … all this stuff is happening from that perspective.”

title_original: ‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The great benefit of having clout in Hollywood — aside from fame, fortune, and a standing reservation at any restaurant in town — is being able to say “no.” You don’t have to take any job that pays. You don’t even have to work year-round. And you certainly don’t have to chase silly trends, like, say — I don’t know — making a comedy that’s also a mystery that’s also a drama ? Beloved, funny folks like Amy Poehler and Mike Schur , who earned a huge chunk of their influence through the indelible sitcom, “Parks and Recreation,” should be able to make anything they want! Any way they want! They earned it!", "links": [{"text": "a comedy that’s also a mystery that’s also a drama", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/shows/how-to-get-to-heaven-from-belfast-review-derry-girls-netflix-mystery-1235178884/"}, {"text": "Amy Poehler", "url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CC9-vvkvrW0"}, {"text": "Mike Schur", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/the-good-place-explained-michael-schur-season-3-1202025660/"}, {"text": "“Parks and Recreation,”", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/commentary/parks-and-recreation-nearly-canceled-comedy-classic-1235189161/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "They should never have to take a comedy, tack on a mystery, and toss in a little bit of romance and drama just to ensure their project appeals to every potential Peacock subscriber (aka anyone with a credit card). They should never need to concede to a process that slowly but inevitably turns their original idea into an amorphous, half-hearted, and crushingly unfunny new thing that barely resembles the kind of comedy that made them kings.", "links": [{"text": "Peacock", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/peacock/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2306106159.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "President Trump at a news briefing on November 20 in Washington, D.C.", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screen-Shot-2026-08-24-at-3.42.53-PM.png?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "'Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall'", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And yet. “Dig.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Far be it from me to know what exactly went wrong with Schur and Poehler’s new series, but something did, unfortunately, go wrong. Each 32-35 minute episode strains to wrap up plots that limp to the finish line. Narrative momentum only exists from the minor twists revealed in the final seconds — then the credits roll, the “up next” button lights up, and your natural curiosity over what happens next wins out over your desire to scroll for something better. Worst of all, everything is “light”: The tone is light, the jokes are light, the mystery is light, the drama is light, even the lighting is light. (It’s so bright, all the time, even at night! ) Watching “Dig” is like bearing witness to dwindling interest: Whatever originally compelled the “Dig” team to adapt Kate Myers’ 2023 novel, “Excavations” gets spread so thin across the disparate parts of this broad adaptation that there’s almost nothing left."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nothing, that is, but the stars. Poehler leads an affable cast (astutely assembled by casting directors Allison Jones and Emily Buntyn) as lead archaeologist Elise, a devoted digger (no, not that kind ) whose decades in the dirt have earned her respect and admiration but also turned her cynical and closed-off. She’s an accomplished expert in the field who’s been waiting to run her own site for years, working diligently under the tutelage of beloved British professor Neville Wycombe ( Hugh Laurie ), but events have conspired to keep her from the top job.", "links": [{"text": "Allison Jones", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/consider-this/allison-jones-acting-barry-curb-your-enthusiasm-casting-director-1234751963/"}, {"text": "that kind", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/digger-movie-review-tom-cruise-1235219051/"}, {"text": "Hugh Laurie", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/hugh-laurie/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The most obvious issue is also the simplest: Neville has repeatedly promised to retire, only to rescind that promise when it comes time to make it official. This year he swears he’ll step down for real , but Elise knows better than to buy-in, especially when her informal audition (giving the welcome speech to a group of undergrads they call Ugs) exposes her greatest weakness: She’s not an inspiring leader. “I know your default setting is ‘tough love,'” Neville tells Elise, “but please learn to give people some grace.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That advice is put to the test when Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), Elise’s flaky former protégé, shows up at the dig site after abandoning her post five years prior without so much as a goodbye. Returning with a questionable back tattoo that reads “a traveler on the adventure of life” and without any luggage, directions, or direction (as in, for her life), Dylan is a messy 29-year-old trying to sort things out as she turns 30. Luckily, she meets the too-put-together-for-her-own-good Clare (Antonia Thomas), a 39-year-old head preservationist who’s secure in her calling, engaged to Dylan’s ex-boyfriend Gary (Jon Pointing), and always dressed to the nines. (Surprise, surprise: Clare comes from money.)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The two will learn from each other, just as they’ll each learn from Elise, but they should all take more cues from Patty Borkman (Fina Strazza), the 19-year-old intern who’s assigned to be Neville’s assistant. That’s, in part, because Patty is the youngest and eagerist of a central foursome neatly divided by decades (did I mention Elise is 49?), but more so because Patty — as you may have guessed by her last name — is a fizzy vat of quirky energy that Strazza impressively dissipates into a charming, fresh , coming-of-age character."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Dig-series-Dylan-actor-Geraldine-Viswanathan-Patty-actor-Fina-Strazza.jpg?w=650", "alt": "DIG cast includes Geraldine Viswanathan as Dylan, Fina Strazza as Patty in the new show on Peacock", "caption": "Geraldine Viswanathan and Fina Strazza in ‘Dig’ Courtesy of Colleen Hayes / Peacock", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Patty’s voice sounds like a shy version of Cristin Milioti’s adult baby from “30 Rock.” She wears silly hats, can’t drive, and struggles to stick up for herself. She kinda, sorta believes she’s a demigod (after reading one of Neville’s books on Greek mythology as a kid), and she’s always been an outcast (for these reasons and more). Watching Patty come into her own — in ways both delightfully weird and universally endearing — is the most rewarding and compelling aspect of “Dig”; a strange, distinctive spark that could grow into a roaring fire if the series continues (and learns from its strongest asset).", "links": [{"text": "adult baby", "url": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cm8eFZT3Y-c"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But that’s a big “if.” The first season (consisting of 10 episodes) pivots around the four women finding a rare statue and making the questionable decision to keep it secret from Neville. At the time, they say it’s because their boss takes credit for everything, and they want something that’s just their own, but that contention doesn’t hold up to scrutiny as the season progresses because Neville doesn’t hold up to scrutiny as the season progresses. Neville is whoever he needs to be in any given episode — a mentor, an oppressor, a goofball, a stick in the mud, a nice old man, and a villainous monster — and while Laurie can pivot with the best of them, his inconsistent character development betrays a show that’s hesitant to commit to much of anything."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The love triangle between Gary, Dylan, and Clare fizzles out without any substantial conflict. Elsewhere, an inappropriate crush is introduced and tossed away without consequence. Great guest stars like Jason Mantzoukas (a local looter) and Max Greenfield (as a sketchy art dealer) feel like they were hired for arcs that ended up getting cut, while regulars (like Gary) can feel adrift in their ample, listless screentime. Premises primed for comic hijinks never get there, mysteries teed up for suspense are left slack, and relationships that should create a little friction when brought together instead find a way to slide off each other without anything sticking."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Poehler, at the center of it all, is a problem. While it’s theoretically interesting to see the former Leslie Knope take the opposite tact — playing another hard-working public servant (every artifact they uncover remains in Greece) only without the unbridled optimism — Elise’s glum demeanor limits her ability to crack jokes, stir passion, and generally light up a scene.
